question.text: Under Modern Portfolio Theory, an investor is offered a risky portfolio with an expected return of 12% and the risk-free rate is 7%. The investor's Certainty Equivalent Rate (CER) is calculated as 6%. What can be concluded about this investor's risk preference and investment decision?

answer.text: The investor is risk-neutral and will be indifferent between the risky portfolio and risk-free asset
The investor is risk-seeking and will accept the risky portfolio
The investor is risk-averse and will reject the risky portfolio since CER is below the risk-free rate
The investor is risk-averse but will still accept the risky portfolio since expected return exceeds the risk-free rate

explanation.text: The Logic: When the CER (6%) is below the risk-free rate (7%), the investor is sufficiently risk-averse to reject the risky portfolio. The CER represents the guaranteed return the investor would accept in lieu of the risky portfolio; if it is less than the risk-free rate, the risk-free asset is preferred. A risk-neutral investor would have CER equal to expected return (12%), and a risk-seeking investor would have CER greater than the expected return. The Trap: Option D is tempting because the risky portfolio's expected return (12%) exceeds the risk-free rate (7%). However, CER already incorporates the investor's risk penalty, and when CER is below the risk-free rate, the guaranteed rate dominates. Note: CER, rather than expected return alone, is the appropriate yardstick for deciding whether a risk-averse investor should hold a risky asset.
